s14b.slug: SATURDAY · 9:05 PM · LE MARIN — THE LAPTOP
body: They eat the first panful anyway. It survived; it sat in its copper through the whole thing, going on in its butter, and the waiter spoons it into two dishes with the gravity of a man serving the last of the rations, and it tastes faintly of smoke and very much of rum, and it is the best thing Jack has put in his mouth since Christmas. The waiter brings two coffees, and wipes out the pan, and does it all again from the butter up. This time the flame goes up a sensible height and comes down, and the room, watching, gives it a small round of applause, and the waiter inclines his head to the room.
Lena tastes the second one with her eyes shut. She opens them.
“Too much cinnamon,” she says. “Brennan’s would *weep*.”
“It’s the same pan.”

“It’s the same pan and a different man’s nerve. The first one he made for the room. This one he made for the fire marshal.” She takes another spoonful, a big one. “Brennan’s has been doing this since before my daddy was born, Youngstown. They light it like they mean it and they put it *out* like they mean it.”
“So it was done properly the first time,” he says.
“The first time it set the table on fire.”
“You just said a thing’s properly done if it’s done like you mean it. He meant it. He meant it all over the roses.”

“I said that about *Brennan’s*.” She points her spoon at him. “Properly is the form, Jack. You can do a thing in the right form and have it go wrong on you, and it’s still been done right. A Mass said by a priest with a head cold is a Mass.”
“So you’re saying tonight went right.”

She opens her mouth and shuts it. She has walked herself, in her mother’s navy dress, straight into the corner, and he can see on her face that she knows it, and he watches her look round the corner for a door.
“I’m saying,” Lena says, “that the *form* was —” She stops. “Lord. You did that on purpose.”
“I had a list.”
“You had a *list*?”
“Reservation. Jacket. Iron something. Flowers. Cab. Pay.”

“And you set fire to number four.” She puts the spoon down so she can laugh properly. “Fine. You win. I hate it, and I want it known that I hate it.” She picks the spoon back up. “Flowers was number *four*?”

body.text: She looks at him over the dish for a while, with the spoon in her mouth, and takes it out. “‘Not anybody’s anything,’” she says. “I said it to the mirror for a week.”
She looks at him over the dish for a while, with the spoon in her mouth, and takes it out. “‘A dishwasher from Ohio,’” she says. “My mother laughed for ten minutes.”
She looks at him over the dish for a while, with the spoon in her mouth, and takes it out. “‘Be with me,’” she says. “I had a speech ready for a no, and you didn’t give me one.”

She sees the card. It’s still lying where it fell, face up on the wet cloth beside the black curl of the cellophane, St. Francis and his bird and *In Loving Memory*, and she reaches over and turns it to the lamp with one finger and reads it. Walter J. Pruszynski. 1921–2009. St. Joseph the Worker. She looks up at the jacket, and at Jack, and puts it together, and her face goes very soft and very interested at once.
“He was in your *pocket*?”
“Nine dollars,” Jack says. “He came with it.”

Lena puts her spoon down and folds her hands on the edge of the table, so he puts his down and folds his. Over the second Bananas Foster in Le Marin, low, with the bananas going cold in their dishes, she says, “Eternal rest grant unto him, O Lord,” and he says, “and let perpetual light shine upon him,” and they both cross themselves. It is the funniest thing either of them has done all year, and neither of them laughs. Walter was born in 1921. He went out to dinner in that jacket, probably, a hundred times, and nobody ever set the table on fire for him.
“He’d have liked the fire,” Lena says, and slides the card across the cloth, and Jack dries it on his napkin and puts it back in the breast pocket where it lives.

body: He tells her he heard it. Wednesday. Laney going past the glass with the laptop, and *Oh my God, Lena*, coming up the stairwell after her. He was on the landing.
Lena sets the spoon down in the dish, carefully, and sits back.

“Then you heard Laney,” she says. “You didn’t hear me. Let me tell it.” And she tells it with her hands. “No knock. There is never a knock. The door just *happens*, and there is Laney Price in the cowboy-boot pajama pants and a T-shirt to her knees, holding the laptop out in front of her flat, like a birthday cake with every candle going, and her BlackBerry in her teeth, *buzzing*, Jack, it’s buzzing against her teeth, and she takes it out of her mouth to say, ‘Oh my God. *Lena.*’” Lena does the Highland Park vowels, all of them. “And I said, ‘Laney, I gave it up for Lent,’ and she said, ‘Then *listen*,’ and read it to me. Out loud. With the little broken heart.”
He can see Laney’s face. He can see it exactly. He has never seen it.
“And then what?”
Lena looks at the tablecloth. Her hands come down off the air into her lap.

“I sat down,” she says. “On the floor. Between the beds. I had my coat on still, I’d just come in, and I sat down on the floor of 217 in my coat. I don’t know why. My legs did it.” She turns her coffee cup a little on its saucer. “And Laney shut the laptop and sat down on the floor with me. She didn’t say anything. Laney Price. Not one word, for I don’t know how long. Then I got up and went to the five-fifteen at St. Brendan’s, and I lit two candles.”
“Two?”
She looks up at him.
“One’s not your business,” Lena says.

The bill comes in a leather folder, carried by the maître d’ himself. Seventy-one dollars and forty cents. Jack takes out the envelope, Gloria’s gumband and all, and opens it on his knee under the table, and then gives up on the knee and counts it out on the cloth, because there is no other way to do it: fives, and then ones, a great many ones, soft from the tip jar, in a stack beside the coffee cups. Lena watches him do it with her chin on her hand and doesn’t help, and doesn’t look away either.
The maître d’ takes the folder. He glances at the ruined end of the table, at the drowned roses, at the brown stain the shape of Lake Erie where the cellophane went.
“The tablecloth,” he says, without any expression at all, “is on the house.”

body.text: When he’s gone Jack tips the way Theo told him to on Tuesday, like a man who has washed dishes, *which is to say obscenely*: the twenty folded into quarters by somebody who meant it as a secret, and five fives on top of it, and then ones, until Lena reaches across and puts her hand over the envelope.
body.else: When he’s gone Jack tips the way the Anchor taught him: two twenties, near enough, under the saucer of his cup — the one twenty in the envelope, folded into quarters by somebody who meant it as a secret, and four fives to make the other. He knows who picks up the saucer at the end of the night. He has been that man since January.

body: Lena gets her coat from the girl at the check, who hands it over like a prize. Jack gathers the roses up off the window edge of the table, drowned and smelling of rum, and wraps them in a Le Marin napkin because the cellophane is gone. At the door she takes his arm for the heels, and he holds the door, and they go out of the warm long room onto the boards.

s15.slug: SATURDAY · 9:50 PM · THE WHARF, WALKING IN
body: The night has come clear and hard while they were inside. The lamps go down the wharf toward town in a row, each with its own small cone of light on the planks, and past the rail the harbor lies black, and the boats in the marina sit on it with their masts up, and somewhere among them a loose halyard is ringing against aluminum, steady, like a spoon on a glass for a toast nobody gets up to make.

Two boards out from the door Lena stops, puts a hand on his shoulder, and steps out of Laney’s heels. One, and then the other. She picks them up by the straps and hangs them off her fingers, and stands there on the boards in her stockings, two inches shorter, and lets out a sound that has the whole evening in it.
“*Oh*, that’s better,” she says. “Sweet suffering Saint Sebastian, that’s better.”
The planks are cold enough that he can see her feel it. She doesn’t put the shoes back on.

They walk in toward town. The roses go in the crook of her arm, wrapped in their napkin, dripping a little down the navy, and the shoes swing from her other hand, and his hands are in the pockets of the jacket because they have to be somewhere. The boards are uneven. She walks them like she owns them, and every so often her stockinged foot finds a nail head and she says something low in French.
“Tell me the truth,” she says. “The French.”
“Library book.”
“*Which* library book.”

“It has a woman on the cover in a beret. She’s holding a baguette like she’s going to hit somebody with it.” He’s been carrying it on the 11 since Tuesday inside his Oceanography binder so nobody would see. “I practiced on the Hobart. Rudy thinks I’ve been having some kind of episode.”

Lena stops in the middle of the boards and puts the hand with the shoes over her eyes. “*Pour moi*,” she says, in a voice from somewhere between Paris and Glenwood Avenue, deep and slow and terribly sincere, “*le canard.*” And she does the waiter, too, the little bow, the kind English: “The duck. Very good, sir.”
“He was being nice.”

“He was being *heroic*.” She takes her hand down, laughing. “You ordered the duck in French from a man who speaks French, and he let you. That man should be a saint. I’m going to write to the archbishop.”
“You said *s’il vous plaît* like you were born on a boat.”

“I grew up on the bayou, Jack. Half of everybody I know was nearly born on a boat.” She puts her arm through his, shoes and all. “It was a very good duck order, Jack. I’ve never been prouder of anybody in my life.”

Near the foot of the wharf the Anchor’s windows come up on the right, yellow and steamed at the corners, the counter running the length of them and three fishermen on stools with their backs to the harbor. Gloria is behind the counter with the coffeepot. She looks up as they go by. She sees the roses and the shoes and the jacket and the girl in her stocking feet, and she lifts her free hand to the glass, and keeps it there a moment, and goes back to pouring. Jack lifts his hand back. Lena lifts the roses.

There’s no moon. There will be later; there isn’t now. The light is the lamps and the Anchor and, across from it, the bus shelter, lit up white like a fish tank, with a schedule taped inside the glass, and empty.

The 11 comes at twenty to eleven, late, and they haven’t minded. It’s nearly empty: a man asleep against the back window in a Carpinteria Warriors jacket, a woman with a laundry bag between her feet. The driver looks at Lena’s stockings and the shoes in her hand and the roses, and looks at Jack in the jacket, and takes the fare in change without a word, and pulls out before they’ve sat down. They sit down anyway, hard, together, and Lena laughs.

The bus goes up Mission Street under the lights. She turns sideways on the seat, her back against the window, and puts her bare feet up on the edge of the seat beside his leg, and leans her shoulder into his. The cold comes off the glass behind her. Her hair has given up entirely now and is down on both sides. She smells of Laney’s perfume and the smoke from the cellophane and rum, and under all of it, of herself.
His hand is on his knee, and it shakes. Not much. He looks at it.
Lena looks at it too.
“Lent?” she says.
“Something else.”

She doesn’t say anything to that. She takes the hand off his knee and holds it in her lap on the navy, on top of the shoes, and the bus goes on up through town, the doors folding open at empty stops and folding shut, past the Mission, past a laundromat lit up with one woman in it folding towels, up the long hill to campus. At the Delgado stop she puts her feet down on the ribbed floor and stands up with the shoes in one hand and the roses in the other, and he gets up after her, and they get off together into Delgado’s circle, her in her stocking feet on the curb, him with his hand out for the shoes she won’t give him.

s15a.slug: SATURDAY · 11:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — FORM ONE
body: The sophomore on the front desk, the one who wrote *7:00 DELGADO CIRCLE — COSTIGAN* on a Post-it four hours ago, looks up from her organic chemistry as they come through the lobby: the jacket, the girl in her stocking feet with a pair of heels in one hand and an armful of drowned roses in a napkin in the other, both of them smelling like a rum cake. She looks down again at once and turns a page she hasn’t read.

The stairwell at eleven on a Saturday is between shifts: the people going out have gone, and the people coming in haven’t yet. The tube light hums over her landing. The wired glass on two is black, with the hall beyond it dim, and the concrete smells of somebody’s microwave popcorn from an hour ago.

They come up the flight from the ground floor without saying anything, her in front of him in her stocking feet, the shoes in one hand and the roses in the other, and at the top she turns round on her landing, and he stops a step below her, which makes them about the same height.

She doesn’t set the shoes down. She doesn’t set the roses down. She stands there with her hands full and looks at him, and he understands she has decided something. Her chin has come up. He has seen it come up like that in 302, right before she stands to speak.
She kisses him.

She closes the last of the distance herself. Her mouth tastes of brown sugar and of the cold off the bus window, and her free hand, the one with the shoes hooked on its fingers, comes up and lies flat on his lapel, the heels knocking softly against his chest.

body.text: Under her palm Theo’s navy is open across the back from the collar down, and he can feel the stairwell air on his shirt through it, and her hand holding the front of it together.
Under her palm is Walter’s herringbone, and under that, in the breast pocket, the stiff square of the card, and he thinks Walter would not mind.
Under her palm is Rudy’s brown, rough and old and too big, and the smell of rum comes up out of the scorched cuff every time either one of them moves.

body: His hand goes to her jaw. He has never put it there. It goes along the line of it under her ear, where her hair has come down, and she leans her face into his palm, and the roses in the crook of her other arm crush a little against him, the wet stems soaking through to his shirt.

He wants her. It is not complicated and it is not quiet. It goes up in him like the flame off the pan, high, for the room, and he stands on the step a little below her with his hand on her face and her mouth on his and the roses wet against his shirt, and it is enough. It is more than he knew to put on a list.

It goes on longer than Sunday on his step. It is not as long as the church steps. When it ends, she ends it, by drawing back not very far, and he hears her take a breath, close enough to feel it, and she stays there with her eyes still shut.
“That was one,” she says.
She opens her eyes.
“Ask me again tomorrow. Properly means not the same night.”

body.text: It’s her line from the church steps, carried up two flights and down a week.

response: “Tomorrow,” he says.

“Tomorrow,” Lena says back, the way a person repeats an address so as not to lose it. She steps back up onto her landing and turns, and goes down the half flight to two with the shoes swinging off her fingers and the roses held up out of the way of the rail, and the wired-glass door on two lets her through and swings to.

He goes up the two flights to four in Rudy’s brown, the cuff singed, smelling of rum.

response: On his own step, third from the top, he stops with one hand on the rail and says it again, to see how it sounds in the empty stairwell. “Tomorrow.” It sounds fine.

She is already going, down the half flight to two, the shoes in one hand and the roses up on her shoulder like a rifle. “In triplicate, Youngstown,” she says, without turning round, and the door on two takes her.

response: Under the light at the top he looks down at himself. A rose petal, crushed dark, is stuck to the lapel where her hand was. He leaves it.

response: “I’d ask you again right now.”
“I know you would,” Lena says. “That’s why it’s tomorrow.” She steps back up onto the landing, and looks at him one more second with the roses against the navy, and goes down the half flight to two.

response.text: He stays where she left him, a step below her landing in Theo’s navy, split down the back and smelling of rum, with brown sugar in his mouth.
He stays where she left him, a step below her landing in Walter’s herringbone, the card back in its pocket, smelling of rum, with brown sugar in his mouth.
He stays where she left him, a step below her landing in Rudy’s brown with the singed cuff, smelling of rum, with brown sugar in his mouth.

response: He listens. Down on two the door of 217 opens on Laney’s voice going up like a siren, and shuts on it, and he is still standing there grinning at the cinderblock when the light over him flickers and steadies.

choices.key: At her landing after the date, Lena kissed you and told you to ask her again tomorrow, and you nodded and let her go.
response: He nods.

She looks at him a long second, the shoes and the roses in her hands, as if he has answered a question she hadn’t asked yet, and got it right. Then she goes down the half flight to two, and on the turn one of Laney’s heels knocks against the rail, a small bright sound, and she says “*Hush*,” to the shoe, and is through the door.

He goes up the two flights to four in Walter’s herringbone, the card back in its pocket, smelling of rum, and doesn’t feel the stairs.
He goes up the two flights to four in Rudy’s brown, the cuff singed, smelling of rum, and doesn’t feel the stairs.

s16.slug: SUNDAY · 7:10 AM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — SOMETHING CAUGHT FIRE
body: Jack has been awake since six, lying on his back on top of the blanket with his hands behind his head, watching the ceiling go from black to blue to the flat clean white of a March morning on the coast, and not thinking about anything you could write down. The eucalyptus outside is full of some bird that has one thing to say and says it.

He can still taste it. Brown sugar, and the cold off a bus window. He has been going over it in order, like a shift at the Hobart, from the cab to the landing, and every time he gets to the fire he has to stop, because he starts laughing, alone, on his back, in a dorm room at six in the morning, and then he has to start over from the cab.
The door opens and Theo comes in.

He’s in last night’s good trousers and a sweater, and the trousers are wet at the hems, dark to the ankle, with damp sand caught in the cuffs. He shuts the door behind him with his heel and stands against it and holds up his iPhone, screen out, at arm’s length, like a cue card.

body.text: SOMETHING CAUGHT FIRE

He sees his navy. Jack hung it last night on the back of the closet door, and it hangs there now in the morning light with its back to the room, the seam open from the collar to the hem like a fish on a dock. Theo crosses the room and stands in front of it, and lifts one edge of the split between finger and thumb, and lets it fall. “It died for love,” he says. “I’ll have it buried at sea.”
body.else: He lifts his head, and sniffs, twice, like somebody walking into a kitchen. His eyes go to the jacket on the back of the closet door, and come back. “Is that *rum*?”

body: He sits down on the end of his bed, facing Jack across the gap, his elbows on his knees and the phone hanging from one hand.
“I only want to know one thing,” Theo says.

response: “Thank you, Theo.”

response.text: “For Tuesday,” Jack says. “The wine list. The bread. All of it. I handed it back like I’d read it.”
“For the jacket,” Jack says. “It went down doing its job.”
“For Friday a week ago,” Jack says. “The eggs. The strings. The bottle.”

response: Theo looks at him across the gap with his chin on his fists. It isn’t the question he asked.

“You owe me a kidney,” he says. It’s his own line, turned the right way round. He lies back on top of his covers with the phone on his chest, and by the time Jack has found his shoes Theo is asleep, which he almost never is.

“Picture it,” Jack says. “A Catholic. A duck. A copper pan. A long room on a pier, since 1971, and a dozen roses with the price on. He orders the duck. He’s been told not to order the duck. Third act, the dessert goes up, the roses go up, and a maître d’ in a dinner jacket comes across the room with a fire extinguisher he never uses, holding it out in front of him like a tray of drinks.”
Theo has lain back on his bed with his eyes shut and the phone on his chest. “And the girl?”
“The girl puts it out with a napkin.”
“I’d see it twice,” Theo says, to the ceiling, and starts laughing with his eyes still closed, quietly, as if the joke is going to be there when he wakes up and he wants to save some.
“Don’t,” Jack says.
Theo looks at him. Then he falls back on the bed and laughs into his pillow, a long helpless muffled laugh with his shoulders going, and it goes on for some time after Jack has got up.

At the mirror on the closet door Jack knots the Confirmation tie for the 11:30, over and under and through, the same tie as last night. Lifting the knot to his collar, he can still smell the rum on it.

s17.slug: SUNDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE FIG TREE
body: The Mary side, halfway up, the aisle end. He’s kneeling when she comes in, and she kneels beside him, and crosses herself, and is quiet, and sits back and puts the lace on her hair, and none of it is an event. It’s Sunday. She is in the pew. A week ago that was a thing he would have walked around for an hour afterward; this morning it’s where she sits.
She’s in flats, and there’s a Band-Aid on the back of one heel above the line of the shoe. He sees it when she kneels.

The church is purple and bare, the flower stands empty, the sun coming blue through the glass and down the fir ribs. Gus brings them up with a Lenten hymn that walks downhill at the end of every line, and Father Osei comes up the aisle behind the cross, and where the Gloria would be there’s only the creak of three hundred people sitting down.

A woman from the Mesa in a camel coat reads Exodus. Moses with the flock, out past the wilderness, and the bush on fire that doesn’t burn up; and Moses going over to look, because who wouldn’t; and the voice out of it telling him to come no nearer. *Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.* And then the name, which isn’t a name, which is *I AM*. The woman reads it in a steady schoolteacher voice and doesn’t try to do anything to it, and it doesn’t need her to.

There’s no Alleluia before the Gospel. Father Osei reads Luke. Some people come to tell the Lord about the Galileans Pilate killed, and the eighteen the tower at Siloam fell on, and he asks them whether they think those people were worse sinners than anybody else, and says no. Then the parable: a man with a fig tree in his orchard that has given him nothing for three years, and he tells the gardener to cut it down, why should it use up the soil. And the gardener says, *Sir, leave it for this year also, and I shall cultivate the ground around it and fertilize it*; and if it bears, good; and if not, then cut it down.
Father Osei comes down to the sanctuary step with his hands folded.

“Notice that the gardener does not ask the owner only to wait,” he says. “He asks for a year and a shovel; mercy, in this parable, has dirt under its nails.” He goes back to his chair. Behind them somebody approves of the length.

In the prayers of the faithful there is one for the people of Chile, a week on: for the dead and for those still digging, and for the ones waiting for news. *Lord, hear our prayer.* Lena bows her head for that one, lower than for the others, and keeps it down through the response.
Two pews up, on the aisle, Kevin is in his good jacket beside Clare Dominguez. At the sign of peace he turns to her and holds out his hand.
“Peace be with you.”

“And also with you,” Clare says, and then she reaches up with both hands and straightens his collar where it’s gone under on one side, quickly, the way you’d fix a picture going by it in a hall. Kevin lets her.
Lena turns to Jack. Her hand is warm from being folded.
“Peace be with you.”
“And also with you.”

It is a handshake. It is the same one as last week, and it is not the same at all, and the church goes on around them, people reaching across pews, an old man turning round in his seat to find the family behind him.

After the dismissal, while Gus plays them out, Jack and Lena go down the side aisle together and out through the doors into the courtyard, where the sun is on the olive tree and the coffee urns are steaming on their table and the sprinkler, for once, is off.

They leave the courtyard with a donut apiece in napkins and walk down Ocean Road toward campus. The Grove is on their left, the eucalyptus shedding its bark in long curls that lie along the shoulder of the road, pink and cream on the inside where the sun gets at them, and the noon light comes down through the leaves in coins. A kid on a skateboard goes by them downhill, crouched, and is gone.

Lena eats her donut in four bites without stopping talking. She has opinions about the homily. She thinks Father Osei should be allowed to preach for nine minutes, once a year, as a treat for everybody. She thinks the woman in the camel coat read Exodus better than any lector at home has read anything in the history of the archdiocese. She’s walking a little careful on the heel with the Band-Aid.

“Laney’s shoes,” she says, when he looks at the heel. “I’m sending her the bill from the podiatrist. I’m going to frame the bill.” She hooks her arm through his for the downhill. “I slept nine hours. I haven’t slept nine hours since my Confirmation. I woke up and I lay there and I thought, *he brought an extinguisher*, and I had to put the pillow over my face so Laney wouldn’t ask.”
“He never used it.”
“That’s what *kills* me.”
At the crosswalk by the bike racks, where the light takes its time, she stops and brushes the sugar off her fingers and looks at him sideways.
“It’s tomorrow,” she says.
It is. He has known it since six this morning. He has the day, and the place, and what he’s going to do about it, and not one word of how to ask.

“Then yes.”

response.text: “That’s two,” she says. “There’s one left. Don’t you dare ask me the third before I tell you to.”

response: He means to kiss her and she gets there first, by a step, quick, her hand on his sleeve.
A blue Corolla coming down Ocean Road slows for them at the crosswalk, though the light is still against them, and the man at the wheel waves them across with a big slow arm, grinning, and they go.

s18.slug: SUNDAY · 6:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — MA
body: Nine-thirty on Glenwood Avenue, and the RAZR goes on the dot. He’s on his own step, third down from four, with his back to the cinderblock.

body.text: “How was Lena’s dinner?” Ma says. She has been saving the name since last Sunday, and she uses it like she bought it.
“How was the dinner?” Ma says. “Friday’s girl.”
“Is it still ‘not yet’?” Ma says.
“It’s a date now, Ma.”
“*Good.* How was it?”

body: “It was good, Ma.”
“Did you iron?”
“I ironed, Ma.”
“What did you iron?”
“The shirt. The oxford.”
“Good.” She waits. She has always been able to wait longer than anybody in the family, and it has always worked. “And?”

So he tells her. The restaurant, the long room on the water, three forks, the duck. The man with the cart and the copper pan. He gets to the roses and the cellophane and the flame going sideways, and his mother says, “*No*,” and he gets to the maître d’ and the fire extinguisher, and he hears the phone go down on the counter on Glenwood Avenue, a clatter, and from a distance, small, his mother laughing. He hasn’t heard her laugh like that since before the plant. Nonna in the other room calling out to ask what, what is it, what happened.
When Ma picks the phone up again she has to stop twice to finish a sentence. “Your *grandmother* —” she says. “Hold on. She wants to know.”
Behind her, close to the phone, an old voice with Calabria all the way through it: “*Mangia?*”
“She wants to know does the girl eat.”
“She ate a whole sole, Nonna. Then she ate dessert twice.”
Ma relays it. There’s a short silence in the kitchen on Glenwood, and then Nonna, from close by: “*Brava.*” It’s the word she has for a good loaf.

“She approves,” Ma says. “She says bring her home.” Then her voice goes practical, the school-secretary voice for the end of a call. “Your birthday’s a Friday this year. St. Joseph. Your grandmother wants to know do they do the table out there.”
“I don’t know, Ma. I’ll find out.”
“Find out. She’ll want to send something. Eat something. Text your father.” And she’s gone.

body: He sends it in capitals, which takes some doing on the RAZR, and sits on his step with the phone open on his knee and the little screen lit, waiting to see what his father does with that.

s19.slug: SUNDAY · 8:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, 4TH FLOOR LOUNGE — BEST PICTURE
body: The fourth-floor lounge has been the Oscars since five-thirty and looks it: popcorn ground into the carpet, a pizza box with one crust in it, two dozen people on the couches and the arms of the couches and the floor, and on the whiteboard by the door Theo’s ballot pool, in three colors of marker, with everybody’s picks down the side and Theo’s name at the top in a box, underlined, with a star. Under *BEST PICTURE* he has written THE HURT LOCKER, and under that, smaller, *(called it in October — ask anyone)*.

body.text: On the corkboard beside it, between a flyer for a ukulele club and a lost-cat sign, somebody has pinned a *Tide* house ad: *THE TIDE WANTS YOUR MEMORIES OF APRIL.*

body: Laney is on the floor in front of the TV in a satin robe over her jeans, conducting a red-carpet review that began some hours ago and has not slowed. She has scored every gown on the night, and she reads her scores off the back of a Domino’s receipt. Kevin is in the armchair beside the couch with Clare Dominguez on its arm. When the camera finds a gown in the crowd with a train that goes on for some time, Kevin says, “Respectfully, I’d admit that train for observation,” and Clare laughs so hard she has to put her face in his shoulder.
Margot is cross-legged at the end of the couch with her notebook on her knee.

Jack is on the couch, in the middle. Lena is beside him with her flats off and her feet tucked under her, and sometime during the last commercial break, without saying anything, she put her head on his shoulder. It’s there now. Her hair is against his neck and his collar, and he can feel the warmth of her through his shirt, and she is watching the television as if this is how she always watches television.
Not one person says a word about it. Laney, on the floor, turns her head, and sees, and turns back to the screen, and her mouth does something heroic and private all by itself.

Best Director goes to Kathryn Bigelow. The lounge cheers, mostly for Theo’s pool. Margot doesn’t cheer. She watches the screen without moving at all, her pen still in her hand, and her face doesn’t do anything, and Jack, from where he is, can see her not doing it.

body.text: She uncaps the pen and writes one line in the notebook, and caps it again.
body.else: The pen stays capped. She doesn’t write anything down.

body: In the commercial Laney gets up onto her knees and leans across the coffee table toward the couch, a woman asking for the popcorn.
“Is there an asterisk?” she says.
Lena doesn’t lift her head off his shoulder.
“There’s an asterisk,” she says.

body.text: Jack looks down, and Lena looks up, and there is the look — the two of them, a second’s worth, over the top of the room, with everything in it they have never once said about the people in it.

body: Laney sits back on her heels. She mouths something across the lounge at Theo, a short word with a lot in it. Theo, in the far armchair, becomes absorbed in a commercial for a hybrid car, with the attention he usually gives Truffaut. In the armchair by the couch Kevin closes his eyes, and keeps them closed until the car has gone.

Best Picture is the last thing. When it goes to *The Hurt Locker*, Theo is on his feet on the seat of the armchair with both arms up, a man who called it in October and is going to be tiresome about it until Easter, and the room is shouting, and Laney is throwing popcorn, and somebody is pounding on the whiteboard.

Lena laughs against his shoulder. He feels it go through her into him. Then she lifts her head and looks at him from four inches off, in front of everybody, the lounge going on around them, and puts it back down.

s19a.slug: SUNDAY · 9:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — THE MINI-FRIDGE
body: He comes down the hall for a pop. Theo is still in the lounge collecting on the pool, going round the couches with a coffee can, and 412 is dark except for the hall light coming in at the door. He doesn’t turn on the lamp. He crouches in front of the mini-fridge under Theo’s desk and opens it, and the little light comes on.

body.text: Theo’s San Pellegrino in its green bottles. The Cool Whip tub from before Christmas, which nobody in 412 is ever going to open. And in the middle, on its side, where Laney laid it down a week ago Friday, the Veuve, corked, the yellow label to the wall.
body.else: Theo’s San Pellegrino in its green bottles, and the Cool Whip tub from before Christmas, and his own cans of pop behind them.

body.text: He takes a can of pop from the back, past the bottle. He looks at the bottle a little longer. He shuts the door on it, and the light goes off inside.
body.else: He takes a can of pop from the back and shuts the door.

body: Standing, he holds the cold can a moment against the inside of his wrist, where the iron got him yesterday at five o’clock, until the burn quiets down; and then he goes back down the hall toward the noise, where she’s saving his place.
